If I may act as the Devil's Advocate:

  1. This is an open door for mob rule. Popularity of individuals will easily sway the moderation of large subs. Most of the subscribers to anything are purely consumers, and go in whichever direction appears to be the popular one because they don't actually care about the issues, only whether there is something for them to consume. Drama is a consumable commodity, and instituting mob wars over ruling stirs up plenty of that.

  2. People put a lot of time and work into subverses, trying to grow and cultivate them into something that gets traffic and posts. There is little incentive to do this hard work only to hand it over to the @system account and potentially lose the very thing that made the subverse grow in the first place.

  3. People don't quit subverses, they quit moderators. Voat is very young and has a chance to do something different than every other site of its kind - it can truly allow the community to curate itself. A proposal was recently made in which the idea of a code change that would neither eliminate moderators, nor give control of all content flow to them was discussed. The essentials are that users would be able to subscribe to moderators rather than just subscribing to subverses. A user who doesn't like the way a particular moderator operates (e.g. what posts and comments they delete) would unsubscribe from that moderator. For the large, default, site branded subverses this kind of strategy could see a lot of benefit - without the need to remove unpopular moderators. This is a potential alternative to the system described by OP.
